name: Crocodile oil skincare

lead: Crocodile oil is a fat extracted from farmed crocodiles, used in traditional medicine for skin conditions and burns and now in some balms and cosmetics. Users apply it to moisturise skin and for anti-ageing, drawing on a fatty acid profile rich in oleic, palmitic and linoleic acids.
Laboratory work includes rat burn-wound studies and antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory tests; a clinical study on ageing skin compared it with a placebo lotion and found both raised hydration.

paras: It is applied topically as a balm or oil, in products ranging from lip balms to large jars. Some brands use it as the main ingredient.
Topical safety data in humans are limited. Crocodile farming raises conservation and animal-welfare debates, and the Nile crocodile is on CITES Appendix II while the Siamese crocodile is endangered.

chain: Fatty acids moisturise and may calm inflammation
angle.text: Users apply crocodile oil as a skin moisturiser and for anti-ageing and scar care, drawing on traditional use and a fatty acid profile compared with human skin oils.

lead: Crocodile oil is extracted from the fatty tissue of crocodiles, mainly from farms in Thailand and other countries [1][2]. It has traditional use for skin conditions, rashes, eczema and wound healing in parts of Africa, and for burns in Chinese and Southeast Asian medicine [1]. Modern products market it as a moisturiser and anti-ageing ingredient.

Its fatty acid profile is rich in oleic, palmitic and linoleic acids [1]. Research includes rat burn-wound studies and in vitro antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory work [3][4][5], plus feeding studies in animals that examine metabolism rather than skin [6][7].
infobox: Crocodile fat (e.g. Crocodylus siamensis, C. niloticus)
Balms, oils, lip balm; about US$4 to US$104 [1]
Nile crocodile CITES Appendix II; Siamese crocodile endangered [1]

paras: The oil is rendered from crocodile fat, with major producers in Thailand, the US, Australia and South Africa [1]. It is used in skincare, cosmetics and leather dressing [1].

Traditional uses include skin conditions in Africa, burns in Chinese and Southeast Asian medicine and 19th-century Ayurveda, and hair growth in ancient Egypt, according to the Wikipedia summary [1]. Cosmetics brands market it for moisturising and anti-ageing [1].

A 2012 study of Nile crocodile oil reported an updated fatty acid profile and antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties [4]. A 2012 rat study found Siamese crocodile oil improved deep second-degree burn healing and reduced scarring compared with controls [3]. A 2021 rat study reported repair effects on burns through growth factor expression [5]. Penetration-enhancement studies have also examined natural oils in topical forms [8]. Oral studies in animals have looked at liver enzymes, gut microbiome and kidney effects; one rat study found high-dose crocodile oil exacerbated diabetic kidney injury [6][7].

A clinical study on ageing skin compared crocodile oil with a placebo lotion; both increased hydration and no improvement in scaliness or elasticity was found, per Wikipedia's summary [1]. Otherwise, studies in the cited literature are in rats, mice and cell models [3][4][5].

Crocodile farming draws conservation and animal-welfare criticism, and vegan or cruelty-free demand has added to it [1]. A PCR assay has been developed to detect crocodile species in commercial products [9].
